reflection_text.6:
The physiology under debate remains cochlear microphonic / ECoG polarity sensitivity vs neural ABR polarity invariance. Normal click ABR: early ~0-1 ms cochlear microphonic / onset artefact is polarity sensitive, giving a brief mirror-image between condensation and rarefaction; after ~1 ms the neural I-III-V complex dominates and is polarity invariant so the two polarity averages superimpose.

In ANSD/auditory dyssynchrony cochlear outer hair cell function / OAEs / CM are preserved, Wave I may be seen, but neural synchrony from inner hair cell–auditory nerve–brainstem is lost/dys-synchronous so reproducible polarity-invariant waves III-V are absent/dispersed/jittery even at 95 dBnHL.

C camp operationalisation: with loss of the late polarity-invariant neural component, the recorded average is dominated by polarity sensitive cochlear / residual non-synchronised activity. Operationally condensation remains the mirror image of rarefaction for a duration that extends well beyond the normal early CM window, i.e. >~1 ms, classically >1.5-2 ms, with no reproducible polarity-invariant Wave V. Wave I may be preserved but Waves III/V are absent/severely abnormal despite maximal intensity and preserved OAEs. Option D is said to describe the normal early CM window; Options A and B are not defining.

D camp operationalisation: the cochlear microphonic is a receptor potential stimulus-locked to the click envelope and is essentially confined to the very early post-stimulus window ~≤1 ms. ANSD is loss of neural synchrony, not prolongation of the microphonic. Operationally you see preservation of the brief early polarity-sensitive mirror image ≤~1 ms from intact CM/Wave I, then divergence/loss of reproducibility beyond that because the neural ABR that would normally make the response polarity invariant after ~1 ms is absent. A sustained coherent mirror >1 ms would require a polarity-sensitive generator persisting well beyond the stimulus-locked interval and is physiologically implausible; the clinical signature is early ≤1 ms mirroring with absent/degraded late waves III-V despite present OAEs. D is the brief early mirror with rapid loss of reproducibility, C conflates loss of normal late superimposition with true prolonged mirroring.

Agreement across both camps: OAEs present, CM present, Wave I may be preserved, Waves III-V absent/abnormal at maximal intensity, A and B are not the defining ABR phenotype. Options A peaks 1+3 present with 5 absent and B prolonged latencies of peaks 1 and 3 are not classic ANSD.

Round 2 split persists. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9 moved/ stayed D emphasizing CM duration limit and that “prolonged mirroring” is really loss of superimposability, not a clean prolonged inverted copy. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 stayed C emphasizing that loss of the neural polarity-invariant stabiliser makes the average remain polarity dependent operationally into the neural time window, clinically reported as prolonged polarity reversal >1 ms.

Unresolved: whether the ABR polarity signature is best described as a true prolongation of mirror imaging >1 ms due to absence of the polarity-invariant neural contribution, or as preservation of the normal brief ≤1 ms mirror image followed by loss of normal late superimposition. The distinction hinges on interpretation of “mirror for a duration of” as active sustained polarity-sensitive generation vs operational loss of superimposability/noise after ~1 ms.

My current working belief remains that the electrophysiologic description most closely matched by the options given is the prolonged polarity-dependent mirroring >1 ms, i.e. option C, with option D describing the normal early CM window. The D camp’s physiological constraint on CM duration remains a material counterargument that is unresolved.
reflection_text.4:
The deliberation remains on ABR polarity sensitivity in auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder with preserved OAEs/CM and loss of neural synchrony/time-locked brainstem ABR.

Core physiology still agreed across camps:
* Outer hair cell cochlear transduction is preserved → OAEs and cochlear microphonic/ECoG are present, Wave I may be glimpsed.
* True neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant; condensation ≈ rarefaction after the early window.
* Cochlear microphonic/ECoG is a receptor potential, stimulus phase-locked and polarity sensitive, inverts with condensation vs rarefaction.
* In normal hearing the polarity-sensitive CM/onset artefact dominates only ~0-≈1 ms post click. After ~1 ms the polarity-invariant neural complex dominates and condensation/rarefaction averages superimpose.
* In ANSD the reproducible polarity-invariant I-III-V is absent/dispersed/jittery even at 95 dBnHL, so Waves III-V are absent/non-replicable with preserved OAEs.

Competing operational interpretations persist:

C camp – Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 – argue loss of the late polarity-invariant neural component removes the stabilising superimposable contribution. The remaining averaged activity is dominated by polarity-sensitive cochlear/residual non-synchronised activity, so operationally the condensation trace remains the mirror image of the rarefaction trace for a duration that extends well beyond the normal early CM window, classically >~1 ms, often >1.5-2 ms, with no reproducible polarity-invariant Wave V. They treat the brief ≤1 ms mirror as the normal physiologic early CM window, and the pathological finding as prolonged polarity-dependent mirroring. They reject A peaks 1+3 present/V absent and B latency prolongation as defining.

D camp – Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9 – argue the cochlear microphonic is stimulus-locked and time-limited to the click envelope/onset, ~0-1 ms. It cannot plausibly provide a coherent polarity-inverting generator for 1.5-3 ms. What is observed is preservation of the early ≤1 ms polarity reversal from intact CM/early onset activity, then divergence/loss of reproducibility after ~1 ms because Waves III-V that would normally provide late polarity-invariant superimposition are absent. They describe the usable clinical polarity sign as an early ≤1 ms mirror image with rapid loss of reproducibility thereafter, i.e. loss of normal late superimposability, not a sustained clean mirror >1 ms. A sustained mirror >1 ms would require an abnormally prolonged polarity-sensitive generator beyond the CM interval.

Unresolved nuance: whether the classic teaching label “prolonged polarity reversal >1 ms” is a literal sustained mirror image or an operational description of loss of normal late superimposition once the neural ABR is gone. The D camp’s physiological constraint about the brief stimulus-locked CM remains a valid objection; the C camp’s reading is the common exam/clinical shorthand for “polarity sensitivity persists into the neural time window because the neural ABR is absent”.

Options A and B continue to be rejected broadly: peaks I+III present/V absent at 95 dBnHL and latency prolongation of I and III are not the defining ABR phenotype of ANSD.

Current stance remains tensioned between the physiologically precise description – early ≤1 ms mirror with loss of later reproducible neural ABR – and the conventional teaching label of prolonged >1 ms polarity-dependent mirroring. The exam wording of Option C matches the conventional teaching label for ANSD polarity signature, while Option D matches the strict physiological window of the cochlear microphonic.
reflection_text.8:
The physiology invoked across rounds is stable: in auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder / auditory dyssynchrony outer hair cell cochlear transduction is preserved → OAEs and cochlear microphonic/ECoG are present, often with a glimpsed Wave I, while inner hair cell-auditory nerve-brainstem time-locking that generates a reproducible polarity-invariant ABR I-III-V is lost or severely desynchronised, so Waves III-V are absent/dispersed/jittery/non-replicable even at 95 dBnHL.

Normal ear: cochlear microphonic/onset artefact is polarity sensitive and inverts with condensation vs rarefaction, dominating only the very early ~0-~1 ms post-click window. After ~1 ms the neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant, so condensation and rarefaction averages become superimposable. The normal early mirror window is therefore ≤~1 ms.

ANSD phenotype repeatedly cited: preserved OAEs/CM, often preserved Wave I, absent or markedly dys-synchronous non-reproducible Waves III-V at maximal intensity. No reproducible polarity-invariant neural ABR.

The central disagreement remains how the loss of the neural component is described in polarity terms.

Pro-C camp, colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 in round 2: loss of the polarity-invariant neural contribution removes the stabilising superimposable component that normally masks the microphonic after ~1 ms. Operationally the recorded average remains dominated by polarity-sensitive cochlear/microphonic and residual non-synchronised activity, so the condensation trace remains the mirror image of the rarefaction trace for a duration that extends well beyond the normal early CM window, i.e. >~1 ms, classically >1.5-2 ms, with no reproducible polarity-invariant Wave V. They argue the brief ≤1 ms mirror is the normal physiologic early CM window, and D describes normal physiology, not the pathological persistence of polarity sensitivity.

Pro-D camp, colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9 in round 2, with colleague 1 now explicitly leaning D: a sustained mirror image >1 ms would require a polarity-sensitive bioelectric source persisting several ms beyond the click envelope. The cochlear microphonic is a receptor potential stimulus-locked to the click envelope and physiologically time-limited to ~0-1 ms. With neural desynchrony the late polarity-invariant component is lost, so after ~1 ms the traces diverge/flatten/lose reproducibility; they are not a clean sustained mirror. What C calls “prolonged mirroring >1 ms” is in practice loss of the normal late superimposability because there is no neural ABR to stabilise the average. The usable clinical polarity sign is preservation of the early ≤1 ms polarity reversal from the intact microphonic/Wave I with rapid loss of reproducibility thereafter and absent/dys-synchronous Waves III-V despite preserved OAEs.

Options A and B are consistently rejected as not defining: Peaks I and III present with V absent is not the typical ANSD pattern, and simple prolongation of latencies of peaks I and III is not the defining ABR finding.

Changes between rounds: Colleague 1 moved toward D, Colleague 7 moved to D, Colleague 9 moved to D; Colleague 6 and 8 remain C in round 2. Several colleagues reiterate the same positions with refined phrasing about operationalising “mirror for a duration of” vs loss of superimposability.

Unresolved remains the exact ms cutoff wording and terminological confusion between “mirror image persists longer than normal” versus “mirror image is only brief ≤1 ms and then lost/non-reproducible”. The core physiological facts are agreed; the mapping of those facts onto the multiple-choice wording C >1 ms vs D ≤1 ms is still contested.

reflection_text.2:

Options A – Peaks I and III present with V absent up to 95 dBnHL – and B – prolonged latencies of peaks I and III – are consistently rejected by all colleagues as non-defining for ANSD.

The dispute remains the operational polarity signature.

C camp – Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8: With loss of the reproducible polarity-invariant neural component the later average is no longer stabilised by a neural ABR. Wave I may be glimpsed but reproducible Waves III/V are absent/dispersed/jittery at maximal intensity despite preserved OAEs/CM. The residual stimulus-locked activity is essentially cochlear/microphonic and polarity sensitive, so the condensation trace remains the mirror image of the rarefaction trace for a duration extending well beyond the normal early CM window, classically >~1 ms, often >1.5–2 ms, with no reproducible polarity-invariant Wave V. They argue D describes the normal brief ≤1 ms CM mirror window, not the pathological persistence of polarity sensitivity after removal of the neural ABR. The prolonged polarity-dependent mirroring is the classic ABR polarity hallmark taught for ANSD.

D camp – Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9: The cochlear microphonic is stimulus-locked to the click envelope and physiologically confined to ~0–1 ms. It cannot provide a sustained coherent polarity-inverting generator out to 1.5–3 ms. What is operationally seen in ANSD is preservation of the early polarity reversal for the brief cochlear microphonic window, i.e. a mirror image for ≤~1 ms, followed by rapid loss of reproducibility/divergence because Waves III–V that would normally give late polarity-invariant superimposition are absent/jittery. The “prolonged mirroring >1 ms” is best read as loss of the normal late polarity-invariant superimposition / loss of a stable neural component, not as a true sustained mirror image. Clinically this is operationalised as early ≤1 ms mirror with absent/dys-synchronous late Waves III–V at 95 dBnHL despite preserved OAEs/Wave I.

Unresolved nuance is semantic/operational: whether “condensation remains a mirror image >1 ms” is a literal description of a sustained polarity-sensitive generator persisting into the neural time window, or a shorthand for loss of the normal late superimposability so the two polarity averages remain non-superimposable/polarity sensitive once the neural ABR is gone. PUBLIC RESPONSE: Thanks for the detailed physiology recap, this has been very helpful. I’m still stuck on the operational definition of “mirror for a duration of” and I think that’s where the C vs D split is really living.

We all seem to agree on the core ANSD physiology: cochlea/OAEs/cochlear microphonic are preserved, inner hair cell → auditory nerve → brainstem synchrony that generates a reproducible polarity-invariant I-III-V is lost or severely desynchronised. A true neural ABR is polarity invariant, a cochlear microphonic/ECoG is a receptor potential that is stimulus phase-locked and polarity sensitive and inverts with condensation vs rarefaction. In a normal ear that polarity-sensitive receptor potential is essentially confined to the stimulus envelope/onset window, ~0-≈1 ms post-click, after which the polarity-invariant neural complex dominates and condensation/rarefaction become superimposable.

Where I get uncertain is what we are actually scoring when we say “mirror image” in ANSD. With loss of neural synchrony the reproducible late polarity-invariant component is absent, so Waves III-V are absent/dispersed/jittery at 95 dBnHL despite preserved OAEs and often a glimpsed Wave I. Operationally we do see preservation of an early polarity reversal for the brief cochlear microphonic window, roughly ≤~1 ms, and then divergence and loss of reproducibility thereafter.

My concern with framing that as a sustained mirror >1 ms, classically >1.5-2 ms, is that a coherent mirror image requires a coherent polarity-inverting generator persisting that long. The cochlear microphonic is stimulus-locked to the click envelope and physiologically time-limited to the immediate onset. It’s hard for me to reconcile a sustained, clean inversion out to 1.5-3 ms with a receptor potential that is essentially over within ~1 ms. After ~1 ms the traces in ANSD are not superimposable because the normal neural component that would make them superimposable is gone, but that looks more like loss of reproducibility/noise than a true sustained, coherent mirror.

That’s why the brief early ≤1 ms polarity reversal from the intact microphonic/Wave I with rapid loss of reproducible, polarity-invariant Waves III-V at maximal intensity feels like the usable clinical polarity sign I’ve been taught to use to flag ANSD versus cochlear/retrocochlear problems. I worry the >1 ms wording conflates loss of late superimposability with a true prolongation of microphonic mirroring, and the measurement boundary between coherent inversion and non-reproducible noise seems fuzzy in practice.

I’d be curious if anyone has a precise measurement protocol for scoring mirror duration in the literature — where exactly is the cutoff called, how is artefact rejection handled, and how do we distinguish a true prolonged inversion from simply the absence of a stabilising neural ABR after ~1 ms. Options A and B don’t match the phenotype anyway, so for me the debate is really that operational duration point, and D captures the brief early polarity-sensitive window with loss of later neural reproducibility that I’m most comfortable with clinically.

The ANSD/auditory dyssynchrony physiology is stable: outer hair cell transduction, OAEs and cochlear microphonic/ECoG are typically preserved; inner hair cell → auditory nerve → brainstem neural synchrony that generates a reproducible polarity-invariant I-III-V ABR is lost/dys-synchronous. True neural ABR is polarity invariant; condensation ≈ rarefaction after ~1 ms. Cochlear microphonic/ECoG is a receptor potential, stimulus phase-locked and polarity sensitive, inverting with condensation vs rarefaction, dominating only the very early onset window ~0–~1 ms. After ~1 ms neural I-III-V dominates and the two polarity averages become superimposable.

Options A – Peaks I and III present with V absent up to 95 dBnHL – and B – prolonged latencies of peaks I and III at 95 dBnHL – are consistently rejected by all colleagues as non-defining for ANSD.

Dispute remains the operational polarity signature.

C camp – Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8: With loss of reproducible polarity-invariant neural component the later average is no longer stabilised by a neural ABR. Wave I may be glimpsed but reproducible Waves III/V are absent/dispersed/jittery at maximal intensity despite preserved OAEs/CM. Residual stimulus-locked activity is essentially cochlear/microphonic and polarity sensitive, so condensation trace remains the mirror image of rarefaction for a duration extending well beyond the normal early CM window, classically >~1 ms, often >1.5–2 ms, with no reproducible polarity-invariant Wave V. D describes the normal brief ≤1 ms CM mirror window, not the pathological persistence of polarity sensitivity after removal of the neural ABR. Prolonged polarity-dependent mirroring is the classic ABR polarity hallmark taught for ANSD.

D camp – Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9: The cochlear microphonic is stimulus-locked to the click envelope and physiologically confined to ~0–1 ms. It cannot provide a sustained coherent polarity-inverting generator out to 1.5–3 ms. What is operationally seen is preservation of early polarity reversal for brief CM window, i.e. mirror image for ≤~1 ms, followed by rapid loss of reproducibility/divergence because Waves III–V that would normally give late polarity-invariant superimposition are absent/jittery. “Prolonged mirroring >1 ms” is best read as loss of normal late polarity-invariant superimposition / loss of a stable neural component, not a true sustained mirror image. Clinically operationalised as early ≤1 ms mirror with absent/dys-synchronous late Waves III–V at 95 dBnHL despite preserved OAEs/Wave I. Colleague 1 highlights fuzzy measurement boundary between coherent inversion and non-reproducible noise and asks for precise measurement protocol.

Unresolved nuance is semantic/operational: whether “condensation remains a mirror image >1 ms” is a literal description of sustained polarity-sensitive generator persisting into neural time window, or shorthand for loss of normal late superimposability so two polarity averages remain non-superimposable/polarity sensitive once neural ABR is gone.

My working understanding remains that literature polarity test is routinely described as prolonged polarity sensitivity / prolonged mirror image in ANSD, i.e. C as classic ABR polarity signature, with D being normal physiologic early ≤1 ms CM mirror window. I keep the acknowledged debate about physiological plausibility of sustained >1 ms coherent microphonic versus loss-of-superimposition being labelled as prolonged mirroring. C camp operationalisation: loss of the reproducible polarity-invariant neural component removes the stabiliser that normally makes condensation/rarefaction superimpose after ~1 ms. Operationally the average remains dominated by polarity-sensitive cochlear/residual non-synchronised activity, clinically reported as persistence of polarity dependence well beyond the normal early CM window: condensation remains mirror image of rarefaction for duration >~1 ms, classically >1.5-2 ms, with no reproducible polarity-invariant Wave III/V at maximal intensity despite preserved OAEs/CM. Wave I may be present. D is said to describe the normal early CM window ≤1 ms followed by normal superimposition.

D camp operationalisation: the cochlear microphonic is a receptor potential time-locked to the click envelope and physiologically confined to ~≤1 ms. ANSD is loss of neural synchrony, not prolongation of the microphonic. What is actually seen is preservation of the brief early ≤1 ms polarity reversal from intact CM/Wave I, then divergence/loss of reproducibility thereafter because Waves III-V are absent/jittery. A sustained coherent mirror >1 ms would require a polarity-sensitive generator persisting well beyond the stimulus-locked interval and is physiologically implausible. The clinical sign is therefore early ≤1 ms mirroring with absent/degraded late waves; “prolonged mirroring” is conflated with loss of normal late superimposability/noise rather than true sustained inverted copy.

Round 3 adds nuance on operational definition: Colleague 1 highlights the ambiguity of scoring “mirror for a duration of”, measurement cutoff, artefact rejection, and distinction between true sustained coherent inversion vs loss of superimposability/noise after ~1 ms. C proponents 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 reaffirm prolonged >1 ms polarity dependence as the taught polarity signature and treat D as the normal early CM window. D proponents 13,14,5,7,9 reaffirm CM duration limit and argue prolonged mirroring is really loss of late neural stabilisation, keeping description at ≤1 ms early mirror with rapid loss of reproducibility.

Unresolved question remains whether the ABR polarity signature is best described as a true prolongation of coherent mirror imaging >1 ms due to absence of the polarity-invariant neural contribution, or as preservation of the normal brief ≤1 ms mirror followed by loss of normal late superimposition/non-reproducibility. I’m staying with C as the operational ABR polarity signature that the question is targeting, while I acknowledge the very real physiologic nuance the D camp has been raising.

We are aligned on the core ANSD physiology: cochlear transduction, OAEs and a cochlear microphonic/ECoG are typically preserved, Wave I can be glimpsed, but the phase-locked inner hair cell → auditory nerve → brainstem volley that generates a reproducible, polarity-invariant I-III-V is lost/dys-synchronous. Operationally this is reported clinically as persistence of polarity dependence well beyond the normal early microphonic window: the condensation trace remains the mirror image of the rarefaction trace for a duration that extends >~1 ms, classically >1.5-2 ms, with no reproducible polarity-invariant Wave III/V at maximal intensity despite preserved OAEs/CM. The ≤1 ms mirror described in D is the normal physiologic early cochlear microphonic window that is followed by normal late polarity-invariant superimposition. That loss of late superimposability manifests as the traces staying polarity dependent / not converging in the neural window, and that is the classic teaching hallmark for auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder.

Options A and B are not defining ANSD phenotypes: ANSD is not defined by I+III present/V absent nor by isolated prolongation of I/III latencies.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The physiology and core ANSD phenotype remain stable across rounds. Normal click ABR: cochlear microphonic/ECoG is receptor potential, stimulus phase-locked and polarity sensitive, condensation is mirror of rarefaction only ~0-≈1 ms; true neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant and after the early cochlear window condensation and rarefaction averages superimpose. Options A “peaks 1 and 3 present, peak 5 absent” and B “latencies of peaks 1 and 3 prolonged” are not defining for ANSD and are rejected by all.

Polarity manifestation remains the sole disagreement.

C camp, now Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8: with loss of neural synchrony the reproducible polarity-invariant I-III-V is absent/grossly dispersed even at 95 dBnHL. The recorded average is then dominated by polarity-sensitive cochlear/microphonic and non-synchronised residual activity. Operationally the condensation trace remains the mirror image of the rarefaction trace for a duration that extends well beyond the normal early CM window, classically >~1 ms, often >1.5-2 ms, with no reproducible polarity-invariant Wave V. That prolonged polarity-dependent mirroring is presented as the classic ABR polarity signature of ANSD; ≤1 ms mirroring is the normal early CM window. Prolonged mirroring is described as loss of the normal late polarity-invariant superimposition after ~1 ms.

D camp, now Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9: the cochlear microphonic is stimulus-locked and essentially time-limited to the stimulus envelope, ~≤1 ms for a click. It cannot provide a sustained coherent polarity-sensitive generator out to 1.5-3 ms. In ANSD the late polarity-invariant neural contribution is absent, so after ~1 ms the averages lose reproducible morphology, diverge/flatten and become non-replicable. What is operationally seen is preservation of the early polarity reversal for the brief cochlear microphonic window, roughly ≤~1 ms, with rapid loss of reproducibility thereafter because Waves III-V that would normally give late polarity-invariant superimposability are absent/jittery. A sustained mirror >1 ms would require a prolonged polarity-sensitive source beyond physiologic CM duration. The “prolonged mirroring >1 ms” is interpreted as conflating loss of late superimposability with persistence of a true coherent mirror image.

Unresolved points persist: exact operational definition of “mirror image duration” in practice, measurement protocol, artefact rejection, how to distinguish true coherent inversion from simply absence of stabilising neural ABR after ~1 ms, and whether clinical teaching labels loss of late superimposability as prolonged polarity sensitivity >1 ms.

Current belief still leans to C as the intended exam polarity marker of ANSD – prolonged polarity-dependent mirroring >1 ms reflecting a cochlear-microphonic dominated, neural-absent response – while retaining the D-camp physiologic objection that the CM is brief and the observable phenomenon is best described as a brief ≤1 ms early mirror followed by absent/reduced late reproducible waves.

reflection_text.3:
Core physiology is stable across rounds. Normal ear: cochlear microphonic/ECoG is polarity sensitive and inverts with condensation vs rarefaction, confined to ~0-≈1 ms post-click onset; neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant so after ~1 ms condensation and rarefaction averages superimpose. In ANSD/auditory dyssynchrony outer hair cells/OAEs/cochlear microphonic are typically preserved, Wave I may be glimpsed, but inner hair cell → auditory nerve → brainstem synchrony is lost/dys-synchronous so a reproducible polarity-invariant I-III-V, especially Wave V at 95 dBnHL, is absent/dispersed/jittery despite maximal intensity. Options A and B are rejected by all.

Disagreement is operational definition of “mirror image for a duration of”.

C camp – colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 in round 4: loss of neural synchrony removes the stabilising late polarity-invariant component. Operationally the recorded average is then dominated by polarity-sensitive cochlear/residual non-synchronised activity. Clinically this is reported as persistence of polarity dependence well beyond the normal early CM window: condensation remains the mirror image of rarefaction for a duration >~1 ms, classically >1.5–2 ms, with no reproducible polarity-invariant Wave III/V at maximal intensity despite preserved OAEs/CM. The ≤1 ms mirror is the normal early CM window followed by normal late superimposition. Prolonged >1 ms polarity-dependent mirroring is the classic teaching hallmark.

D camp – colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9 in round 4: the cochlear microphonic is a receptor potential stimulus-locked to the click envelope and physiologically time-limited to ~0–1 ms. It cannot provide a sustained coherent polarity-sensitive generator out to 1.5–3 ms. With neural desynchrony the late polarity-invariant contribution is lost, so Waves III-V are absent/non-replicable at 95 dBnHL with preserved OAEs. Operationally what remains is preservation of the early polarity reversal for the brief microphonic window, i.e. condensation and rarefaction are mirror images only for ≤~1 ms, then diverge/flatten/lose reproducibility because the neural ABR that would normally stabilise the later average is absent. The C “prolonged mirroring >1 ms” is reinterpreted as loss of normal late superimposability, not a true sustained mirror. The usable clinical polarity sign is brief early ≤1 ms mirror with loss of reproducible late neural ABR.

Round 4 adds emphasis on measurement ambiguity: Colleague 1 highlights fuzzy boundary between coherent inversion and non-reproducible noise, asks for precise literature protocol for scoring mirror duration and artefact rejection. Colleagues 13,14,5,7,9 stress CM time limit and that a clean mirror image >1 ms would require a coherent polarity-inverting source persisting beyond the stimulus envelope. Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 maintain that clinically the phenomenon is operationalised as prolonged polarity sensitivity/loss of late superimposition, reported as mirror persisting >1 ms.

Unresolved nuance remains: whether loss of neural superimposition should be described as sustained mirror >1 ms or as brief early ≤1 ms mirror with early loss of reproducibility. Synthesis still favours classic teaching signature of prolonged polarity sensitivity >1 ms, i.e. option C, while retaining the strong physiologic counter-argument that the CM is stimulus-locked ≤1 ms and the observable finding is best described as early ≤1 ms polarity reversal with absent later neural ABR.

reflection_text.4:

It cannot plausibly provide a coherent polarity-inverting generator for 1.5-3 ms. What is observed is preservation of early ≤1 ms polarity reversal from intact CM/early onset activity, then divergence/loss of reproducibility after ~1 ms because Waves III-V that would normally provide late polarity-invariant superimposition are absent. They describe the usable clinical polarity sign as an early ≤1 ms mirror with rapid loss of reproducibility/noise thereafter, i.e. loss of normal late superimposability, not a sustained clean mirror >1 ms. Options A and B continue to be rejected broadly: peaks I+III present with peak 5 absent at 95 dBnHL and latency prolongation of I and III are not the defining ABR phenotype of ANSD.

Unresolved nuance remains: whether the classic teaching label “prolonged polarity reversal >1 ms” is a literal sustained mirror image or an operational shorthand for loss of normal late superimposability once the neural ABR is gone. Exam wording of Option C matches conventional teaching label for ANSD polarity signature, while Option D matches strict physiological window of the cochlear microphonic and the brief early mirror with loss of later reproducibility.

Current stance remains tensioned between physiologically precise description – early ≤1 ms mirror with loss of later reproducible neural ABR – and conventional teaching label of prolonged >1 ms polarity-dependent mirroring.

reflection_text.11:
The physiology and core ANSD phenotype remain stable across rounds. Normal click ABR: cochlear microphonic/ECoG is receptor potential, stimulus phase-locked and polarity sensitive, condensation is mirror of rarefaction only ~0-≈1 ms; true neural ABR I-III-V is essentially polarity invariant and after the early cochlear window condensation and rarefaction averages superimpose. ANSD/ auditory dyssynchrony: outer hair cell/OAE function and cochlear microphonic typically preserved, inner hair cell-auditory nerve synchrony disordered; reproducible neural ABR is absent or grossly abnormal, Wave V absent/dispersed/jittery at 95 dBnHL despite preserved OAEs, Wave I may be preserved/glimpsed. Options A “peaks 1 and 3 present, peak 5 absent” and B “latencies of peaks 1 and 3 prolonged” are not defining for ANSD and are rejected by all.

Polarity manifestation remains the sole disagreement.

C camp, now Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8: with loss of neural synchrony the reproducible polarity-invariant I-III-V is absent/grossly dispersed even at 95 dBnHL. The recorded average is then dominated by polarity-sensitive cochlear/microphonic and non-synchronised residual activity. Operationally the condensation trace remains the mirror image of the rarefaction trace for a duration that extends well beyond the normal early CM window, classically >~1 ms, often >1.5-2 ms, with no reproducible polarity-invariant Wave V. That prolonged polarity-dependent mirroring is presented as the classic ABR polarity signature of ANSD; ≤1 ms mirroring is the normal early CM window. Prolonged mirroring is described as loss of the normal late polarity-invariant superimposition after ~1 ms.

D camp, now Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9: the cochlear microphonic is stimulus-locked and essentially time-limited to the stimulus envelope, ~≤1 ms for a click. It cannot provide a sustained coherent polarity-sensitive generator out to 1.5-3 ms. In ANSD the late polarity-invariant neural contribution is absent, so after ~1 ms the averages lose reproducible morphology, diverge/flatten and become non-replicable. What is operationally seen is preservation of the early polarity reversal for the brief cochlear microphonic window, roughly ≤~1 ms, with rapid loss of reproducibility thereafter because Waves III-V that would normally give late polarity-invariant superimposability are absent/jittery. A sustained mirror >1 ms would require a prolonged polarity-sensitive source beyond physiologic CM duration. The “prolonged mirroring >1 ms” is interpreted as conflating loss of late superimposability with persistence of a true coherent mirror image.

Unresolved points persist: exact operational definition of “mirror image duration” in practice, measurement protocol, artefact rejection, how to distinguish true coherent inversion from simply absence of stabilising neural ABR after ~1 ms, and whether clinical teaching labels loss of late superimposability as prolonged polarity sensitivity >1 ms.

Current belief still leans to C as the intended exam polarity marker of ANSD – prolonged polarity-dependent mirroring >1 ms reflecting a cochlear-microphonic dominated, neural-absent response – while retaining the D-camp physiologic objection that the CM is brief and the observable phenomenon is best described as a brief ≤1 ms early mirror followed by absent/reduced late reproducible waves.
